lesson.title: Reading the Branches: How to Build and Interpret a Cladogram
lesson.summary: A cladogram is a branching diagram, built using cladistic methods, that represents the hypothesized pattern of common ancestry among a group of organisms based on shared derived characters.
lesson.body:
A cladogram is the diagram that cladistic analysis produces: a branching, tree-like figure in which each branch point, called a node, represents a hypothesized common ancestor, and each line, or branch, leading away from a node represents a separate lineage descending from that ancestor. The tips of the branches, usually drawn at the right or top of the diagram, represent the species or groups being compared. Reading a cladogram correctly means reading it as a hypothesis about the order in which lineages split from one another, based on the shared derived characters used to build it, and it is worth being careful about a few rules that are easy to misread at first.

The most important rule is that a cladogram shows relative branching order, not a strict timeline and not a measure of "how evolved" or "how advanced" any particular species is. Species positioned toward the tip of a longer, later-branching sequence are not more evolved than species that branched off earlier, every species alive today has been evolving for exactly the same amount of time since the root of the tree, they have simply accumulated different traits along the way. A cladogram also does not, by itself, tell you how much time passed between branching events, only some cladograms are drawn with branch lengths scaled to time or to amount of genetic change, plain cladograms only encode order.

Building a simple cladogram follows directly from the method described in the previous chapter. Consider a familiar example built around vertebrates: a lamprey (a jawless fish), a fish with jaws, a frog, a lizard, and a mammal. First, an outgroup is chosen, something known from other evidence to have branched off before all the others, here the lamprey serves that role since it lacks jaws, a trait shared by every other group in the comparison. Comparing the remaining organisms to that outgroup, jaws show up as a shared derived character present in the fish, frog, lizard, and mammal but absent in the lamprey, so those four branch together, away from the lamprey, at the first node. Moving further in, four limbs show up as a shared derived character present in the frog, lizard, and mammal but absent in the jawed fish, so those three branch together at the next node, this group is recognizable as the tetrapods. Moving further still, the amniotic egg, an egg with internal membranes that let the embryo develop without needing external water, is a shared derived character present in the lizard and mammal but absent in the frog, whose eggs still require a moist or aquatic environment, so lizard and mammal branch together at a still later node, this group is the amniotes. The result is a nested pattern, like a set of boxes within boxes, lamprey outside everything, jawed fish outside the tetrapods, frog outside the amniotes, and lizard and mammal as each other's closest relatives among this set, entirely determined by which derived traits are shared at each level.

That worked example also illustrates a distinction worth stating explicitly. Having a backbone is a trait shared by every organism in the example, lamprey included, which makes it a shared primitive character, or symplesiomorphy, relative to this particular group, useful for establishing that they are all vertebrates in the first place, but useless for sorting out relationships within the group, since it does not distinguish any of them from one another. Only traits that are derived relative to the comparison being made, present in some members and absent in others in a way that traces to a real common ancestor, can be used to build the branching structure. This is exactly the shared derived versus shared primitive distinction you will examine in full depth in the next chapter.

Finally, it is worth remembering that a cladogram is always a hypothesis, open to revision if new evidence, a newly discovered fossil, a new trait, or new DNA sequence data, suggests a different branching order fits the data better. This connects directly back to phylogenetics as a field: cladograms are the specific tool most modern phylogenetic trees are constructed and evaluated with, and the tentative, revisable nature of any single cladogram is part of why phylogenetics as a whole is described as reconstructing evolutionary history rather than observing it directly.
